Newly hatched first instar larvae of Chironomus riparius, which we define as the age at birth, were observed to be approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days] old when maintained at a constant water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], a thermal regime that closely matches the laboratory conditions reported in related studies. At this initial stage, the length at birth was measured at 0.09 cm [Lb = 0.09 cm], a modest size that reflects the minimal investment in somatic tissue prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. The eggs from which these larvae hatched had an initial egg ash free dry weight of approximately 1.0 times 10 to the minus 6 grams , a value that is consistent with the low maternal provisioning typical of this chironomid species. This small starting mass underscores the critical importance of rapid feeding success in the first days post-hatch, as larvae must quickly accumulate resources to progress through the early instars. The combination of a short embryonic period and a tiny hatchling mass suggests a life history strategy that prioritizes rapid development over the production of large, well-provisioned offspring.

Under the standard laboratory thermal conditions of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the duration of the first larval instar was precisely 2 days , after which the larvae moulted into the second instar. This rapid progression through instar 1 was followed by an equally brief second instar, which also lasted 2 days , and the third instar showed a slightly extended developmental period of 3 days  at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. A critical life-history transition occurs at the end of the third instar, which we interpret as the attainment of puberty since these early juvenile stages (instars 1 through 3) are non-reproductive. The time since birth at puberty was documented as 7 days [tp = 7 days], meaning that by the end of the third instar, larvae have developed sufficiently to have the physiological capacity for eventual reproduction, even though they have not yet entered the final larval stage. at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]This developmental pace is remarkably rapid among aquatic dipterans.

The fourth instar represents the final larval stage before metamorphosis, and it is during this phase that female larvae attain their maximum size and mass. The female length of 4th instar larvae just prior to pupation was recorded at 1.38 cm , a substantial increase from the hatchling length of just 0.09 cm. At this pre-pupation stage, the maximum observed wet weight of female 4th instar larvae reached 10 times 10 to the minus 3 grams , representing the heaviest body mass recorded during the entire larval phase under control conditions. This dramatic increase in both length and wet weight reflects the intensive feeding activity that characterizes the fourth instar, during which larvae accumulate the nutrient reserves necessary to sustain the non-feeding pupal stage and subsequent adult reproduction. The time at pupation since birth varied considerably depending on the food ration provided to the larvae, revealing a strong plastic response in developmental timing. Specifically, at 21 °C [T = 21 °C], under a feeding regime of 0.1 milligrams per larva per day, pupation occurred at 21 days since birth , whereas at a slightly higher ration of 0.2 milligrams per larva per day, this interval decreased to 12.52 days since birth .

Further exploration of the relationship between food availability and development time at 21 °C [T = 21 °C] revealed a clear negative correlation, with higher rations generally accelerating the time to pupation. At the intermediate feeding rate of 0.3 milligrams per larva per day, the time at pupation since birth was observed to be 12 days since birth  at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. Adults emerging from these pupae had a female dry weight of imago equal to 1.1 times 10 to the minus 3 grams , representing the final adult body mass after metamorphosis.

In addition to the main experiment at 21 °C, a set of extra controls maintained at a slightly cooler temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] provided additional data on adult emergence timing. The time at emergence in these extra controls was recorded at 19.29 days , a value that falls between the faster development seen at 21 °C and the slower pace observed at 15 °C at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This pattern is consistent with the general expectation that within a species' optimal thermal range, higher temperatures accelerate development until a physiological maximum is reached. The female imago dry weight of 0.0011 grams  represents a substantial reduction from the larval wet weight maximum of 0.01 grams, reflecting the loss of water and the histolytic remodelling that occurs during metamorphosis. Comparatively, the initial egg ash free dry weight of approximately 0.000001 grams  illustrates the enormous growth achieved over the larval phase, with a mass increase of over three orders of magnitude. The reproductive adults that emerge are short-lived, with their primary function being mating and oviposition, after which the life cycle begins anew with the deposition of eggs that carry the minute initial egg ash free dry weight necessary to start the next generation.
